title: From Unreliable to Usable: Decomposing Failure Modes and ConfidenceSignals in LLM Entity Extraction — Evidence from Cyber Threat Intelligence

paper.title: From Unreliable to Usable: Decomposing Failure Modes and Confidence Signals in LLM Entity Extraction — Evidence from Cyber Threat Intelligence
paper.abstract: Abstract Audits of large language model (LLM) extraction from full-length documents report severe unreliability, leaving two questions open: what the failures actually consist of, and whether confidence signals can turn unreliable output into usable output. We run a preregistered, fully frozen evaluation of two new-generation low-cost LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash) with a flagship-tier control (GPT-6.1-Sol) on a public corpus of 354 incident campaigns (315 unique reports, 630 model–report evaluations), scoring extraction quality against gold, confidence calibration, and robustness to single-sentence perturbations. Three findings emerge. (1) Unreliability persists across tiers: micro precision is 0.03–0.34 and verbalized calibration error (ECE) 0.53–0.94 across both splits; the gap does not close at the flagship tier. (2) The dominant failure is not hallucination: a full mention census plus a three-tier annotation of 360 sampled candidates (two independent LLM annotators from vendors outside the evaluated set, Cohen’s κ = 0.79 \kappa=0.79 on the preregistered acceptance line, fully disclosed) back-projects to 65.6% background mentions and 19.9% gold-scope gaps, with only 1.2% unsupported candidates. (3) Confidence ranks but does not verify: zero-cost self-consistency-frequency tiering passes a preregistered top-30% precision-gain bar in all six test-split model–type cells (4/6 on train), the zero-cost text-frequency × \times SC combination wins 3, ties 2, loses 1 across cells, yet relation-level counterfactuals on all 45 targets show that a single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in 95.6–100% of cases, and even a background sentence explicitly marked as unrelated still binds a fake vulnerability in up to 26.7% of them. We conclude with a deployment boundary: confidence tiering may set review priorities, never truth.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: When large language models (LLMs) fail at information extraction, the failures are commonly attributed to hallucination. Auditing 315 unique real-world documents (354 incident campaigns; 630 model–report evaluation runs) under a frozen, preregistered protocol with three-tier verified annotation, we find hallucination accounts for only 1.2% of false positives — 65.6% are background mentions : correct strings extracted from the wrong context. We then ask whether confidence signals can still make such a system usable, and show they rank but do not verify : across all 45 counterfactual targets, a single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in 95.6–100% of cases, and one background sentence explicitly marked as unrelated still binds a fake vulnerability in up to 26.7%. These results address a question that outlives any single domain, and the stakes are concrete. LLM-based extraction pipelines for structured threat intelligence claimed 83–97% precision ( Chen et al., 2024 ) ; a critical audit ( Mezzi et al., 2025a ) traced those numbers to toy inputs of 18–106 words and showed that at real scale recall falls below 0.80 and calibration worsens; a reproducibility audit found only 5 of 12 extraction systems re-runnable under their published protocols ( Hakim and Song, 2026 ) . But “unreliable” is a verdict, not a diagnosis — and verbalized confidence is itself severely miscalibrated ( Xiong et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2017 ) . It does not say which part of the pipeline is broken — the model’s faithfulness, the evaluation scope, or the task definition — and it does not say whether the residual uncertainty can be managed. Two questions follow. First, what is the failure made of? Hallucinated content, wrong context, or a mismatch between what the model extracts and what the annotation counts as correct demand different repairs. Second, can confidence make unreliability usable? If high-confidence outputs can be prioritized for scarce human review, an unreliable extractor may still be deployable — unless confidence itself is untrustworthy. We answer both questions on a testbed chosen for measurement quality rather than topical breadth: cyber threat intelligence (CTI) reports, long documents describing intrusion campaigns, from which models must extract three entity types (threat-actor groups, vulnerability identifiers, attack techniques). The domain offers three assets that generic extraction benchmarks rarely combine: a public corpus with gold annotations for 354 campaigns ( Di Tizio et al., 2022 ) , a published critical audit whose protocol and splits we reuse so results are directly comparable ( Mezzi et al., 2025a ) , and a real deployment need — security analysts already triage extracted indicators by confidence, so “usable” has an operational meaning. Our evaluation protocol is explicit and frozen end to end: multiset entity matching with alias equivalence classes, dual confidence proxies (verbalized self-report and self-consistency frequency under 5-sample resampling), preregistered acceptance thresholds, relation-level counterfactual perturbations, and a three-tier annotation study (textual mention / event relevance / relation correctness) on 360 stratified candidates, labeled by two independent LLM annotators from vendors outside the evaluated set with adjudication fully disclosed ( κ = 0.79 \kappa=0.79 on the borderline-excluded preregistered line).

sections.heading: Findings.
sections.text: (1) Unreliability persists across model tiers. Micro precision spans 0.03–0.34 against recall of 0.81–0.99; verbalized ECE is 0.53–0.94 across both splits, and a full-scope control at the flagship tier (GPT-6.1-Sol) shows the same pattern (0.63–0.94). (2) The dominant failure is background contamination, not hallucination. 99.7–99.8% of false positives have an explicit textual source in the report; weighted back-projection of the three-tier annotation yields 65.6% background mentions and 19.9% gold-scope gaps against 1.2% unsupported candidates. (3) Confidence signals decompose into separable, entity-type-dependent properties. SC frequency passes a preregistered ranking bar in all six test-split model–type cells (4/6 on train, with both vulnerability cells just under the line); controlling for text frequency, its partial correlation with correctness is significant in 6/6 groups ( r = 0.30 r=0.30 – 0.43 0.43 ); mention strength tracks event centrality for actors while sampling stability tracks correctness for vulnerabilities and techniques. (4) No confidence signal measures truth. A single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in 95.6–100% of 45 counterfactual targets; verification signals — self-run or third-party — inherit the same blindness; repairs only help when matched to the failure mode, ranking gains transfer to a newer corpus, and thresholds must be recalibrated per corpus.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: This is a systematic evaluation study: model choices and prompting configurations are experimental settings, ranking heuristics are baselines, error analysis and counterfactuals are the core explanation, and repair experiments serve the boundary characterization. The contributions are three: • A reproducible reliability measurement. To our knowledge (as of 2026-10, within audited coverage), the first evaluation framework merging multiset PRF with alias equivalence classes, dual-proxy calibration, three-tier evidence annotation, and preregistered thresholds into one explicit, frozen protocol — executed on the public audit corpus as a direct response to the reproducibility audit above. All protocol, code, and frozen evaluation outputs accompany this preprint and will be made public; an anonymized copy is additionally available to reviewers as supplementary material. • A quantified failure-mode decomposition. A full-scope mention census plus a preregistered three-tier annotation study locating 85.5% of the false-positive mass in background mentions and gold-scope gaps, against 1.2% hallucination — reframing “LLMs hallucinate entities” as “LLMs over-attend to context”. • A tested deployment boundary. Evidence across confidence signals from self-report to third-party verifiers that ranking benefit is real, signal–type matching matters, calibration scope matters, and no tested signal survives relation-level counterfactuals; ranking gain transfers to a newer corpus while thresholds must be recalibrated.

sections.heading: Calibration and verbalized uncertainty.
sections.text: Classical calibration is measured by ECE and reliability curves ( Guo et al., 2017 ) ; for LLMs, verbalized confidence is often miscalibrated ( Xiong et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2023 ) , sampling consistency carries partial signal ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Kadavath et al., 2022 ) , and selective prediction formalizes the risk–coverage trade-off our tiering analysis instantiates ( Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017 ) . We add a three-way distinction — output consistency , ranking benefit , and probabilistic calibration are different quantities that must not be conflated — and test all three against counterfactual ground truth.

sections.heading: LLM-based extraction from threat intelligence.
sections.text: Structured extraction from CTI reports attracted rapid LLM adoption ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Mouiche and Saad, 2026 ; Bouchiha and Blanc, 2026 ) alongside benchmarks ( Alam et al., 2024 ; Ji et al., 2024 ; Alam et al., 2025 ; Ryan et al., 2026 ; Valletta et al., 2026 ) and corpora ( Di Tizio et al., 2022 ; Ech-Chammakhy et al., 2025 ; Das et al., 2026 ) . A critical audit ( Mezzi et al., 2025a ) overturned headline extraction numbers by exposing scoring loopholes and finding LLMs unreliable with overconfidence; follow-ups target pipeline dependencies ( Berriche et al., 2026 ) , automated TTP and strategic-intelligence extraction ( Cheng et al., 2026 ; Ech-Chammakhy et al., 2026 ) , agentic KG construction ( Li et al., 2026 ) , calibrated verification services ( Vasan et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) , and corpus fragmentation ( Suarez-Roman et al., 2026 ) . Reproducibility audits question KG-construction pipelines ( Dinis et al., 2025 ; Hakim and Song, 2026 ) , and systems such as CTINexus ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) have been re-examined under stricter scoring; Chen et al. (2024) systematizes the application landscape. Our work is a systematic evaluation study on the audit’s own public corpus: we reuse its splits for comparability, and extend the audit line from “unreliable” to a measured, preregistered account of what the unreliability consists of and where confidence helps.

sections.heading: Failure-mode analysis of extraction.
sections.text: Prior CTI work reports misses, over-extraction, and misbinding qualitatively ( Alam et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Mezzi et al., 2025b ; Heo et al., 2026 ) . We quantitatively decompose false positives into mention-level and event-level layers with a preregistered three-tier annotation, and separate hallucination (1.2%) from background contamination (65.6%) and gold-scope gaps (19.9%).

sections.heading: 3.1 Task, corpus, and models
sections.text: Given a full-length CTI report, the model extracts three entity types: threat-actor groups (APT), vulnerability identifiers (CVE), and attack techniques (AV, MITRE ATT&CK-style names ( Strom et al., 2020 ) ). We use the public Di Tizio corpus ( Di Tizio et al., 2022 ) under the exact campaign-level 70/30 split of the critical audit ( Mezzi et al., 2025a ) : 354 campaigns (248 train / 106 test at campaign level), 315 train and 93 test reports per model — the same report split reused for both models, for 630 model–report runs in total; Table 1 reports the test split. Gold follows the corpus’s STIX 2.1 structure ( OASIS, 2021 ) and marks primary entities per campaign. We evaluate two new-generation low-cost models (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash — the cheapest “flash” service tiers of their vendors) as subjects and GPT-6.1-Sol as a flagship-tier full-scope control; all runs use frozen prompts, segmentation (cap 40k tokens, overlap 800), temperature-0 extraction with 5-sample self-consistency (SC) resampling (T = = 0.7) per segment. Every reported number is regenerated from frozen batch outputs; the pipeline records gateway and model identity per call (6,048 used segment-level calls on the main table; full call/token accounting in the appendix).

sections.heading: Multiset matching with alias equivalence classes.
sections.text: Predictions and gold are matched as multisets under type-specific normalization: alias equivalence classes with word/digit boundaries (APT), fault-tolerant CVE regexes covering PDF mojibake separators and legacy CAN- prefixes, and a conservative 13-value AV synonym table. This counts every mention as a prediction while gold lists primary entities — a deliberately strict-on-the-model scope whose FP semantics is disambiguated by the annotation study (§ 4.2 ).

sections.heading: Confidence signals.
sections.text: (1) Verbalized : the model’s self-reported 0–100 confidence; (2) SC frequency ( sc_freq ): the share of 5 resamples reproducing the entity — a zero-extra-cost measure of output consistency; (3) text frequency : the count of the entity string in the report, a black-box signal requiring no logits. Their rank-percentile mean forms the zero-cost combination textfreq_sc ; two external verifiers (self-verification and a third-party calibrated decision model) are evaluated against these in § 4.4 .

sections.heading: Preregistered acceptance.
sections.text: Before evaluation we registered: a tiering bar (top-30% confidence-bucket precision ≥ \geq overall + 0.10 +0.10 ), an annotation agreement line ( κ ≥ 0.7 \kappa\geq 0.7 ), and a hypothesis register (H1–H6) separating measured claims from pending ones. Failing a registered bar must be restated as a negative result.

sections.heading: 3.3 Three-tier annotation of sampled candidates
sections.text: To separate what the model extracted from what the annotation counts , all evaluation units of the test split were partitioned by a deliberately lenient mention detector into TP / FP-mentioned / FP-unsupported, and a 360-row stratified subsample (60 per model × \times type; the FP-unsupported stratum fully sampled, the rest balanced across SC-frequency tertiles) was labeled on three tiers: L1 textual mention (does the string appear), L2 event relevance (does it belong to this incident, not background or related work), L3 relation correctness (is the binding and attribution right). The second-annotator role was filled by two independent LLMs (kimi-k3, minimax-m3; neither vendor is among the evaluated models ) under a frozen prompt with temperature 0 and golden-item gating; 36 hard disagreements went to a third adjudicator model and 27 borderline items to a conservative rule resolving toward the model-unfavorable side. Agreement is κ L ​ 2 = 0.68 \kappa_{L2}=0.68 three-class, 0.79 excluding borderline (meeting the preregistered 0.7 line), κ L ​ 3 = 0.74 \kappa_{L3}=0.74 . Stratified sampling weights back-project row-level statistics to the full FP composition (§ 4.2 ). The mechanism is disclosed as LLM-assisted dual annotation throughout — never as two human annotators.

Calibration is worse: mean verbalized confidence sits at 80–90+ against unit-level accuracy of 0.05–0.32, and test-split verbalized ECE reaches 0.59–0.88 (CVE: 0.84–0.94), more severe than the critical audit’s zero-shot scope ( Mezzi et al., 2025a ) . sections.heading: 4.2 Finding 2: failures are background contamination, not hallucination
sections.text: A full-scope mention census over all evaluation units — type-adaptive, deliberately lenient detection so that “unsupported” is a lower bound — shows that 99.7% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) / 99.8% (GLM-5.3-Flash) / 99.7% (GPT-6.1-Sol) of CVE false positives have an explicit textual source in the report; unsupported output is at most 0.2–11.2%. The three-tier annotation (Table 2 ) turns this census into an event-relevance-layer quantification: back-projected by sampling weights, 85.5% of the full FP composition (across all three entity types) is background mentions (65.6%) plus gold-scope gaps (19.9%) — entities the report genuinely mentions and that are event-relevant, but which fall outside the primary-entity gold set — while unsupported phantom candidates are only 1.2% (the unweighted 10.3% is inflated by the fully-sampled stratum). Confidence separates the FP mass by nature: rows in the high SC-tertile are event-relevant in 62% of cases (mostly scope mismatch — the model got the event right, gold does not include it) versus 26% in the low tertile, while 23% of high-confidence gold rows are judged not event-relevant — the scope gap is bidirectional (gold itself has boundaries). The same decomposition holds on a newer 2022–2025 corpus (annotation-derived gold, κ = 0.53 \kappa=0.53 borderline-excluded — Limitations), where relation-level errors ( L3=no ) are entirely absent and FPs are again dominated by background mentions (51.2%). Relation-level KG alignment completes this picture: aligning extracted relation triples against the gold graph yields F1 of only 0.05–0.33 (flagship CVE P 0.049 / R 0.750 / F1 0.092 — precision below both flash tiers with recall on par), because one extra entity is one FP at the entity level but a spurious edge at the graph level — graph quality must be scored at the relation level , not by entity counts or visual inspection. Relation misbinding is a 1-row residual in natural output. The reading is blunt: the reliability problem of modern LLM extraction on long documents is not a faithfulness problem. The models almost never invent entities; they report strings whose truth they cannot adjudicate against this event — “mentioned” is mistaken for “used”. Repairs and deployments should therefore target context disambiguation and review prioritization, not factuality.

sections.heading: 4.3 Evidence faithfulness: outputs are weakly anchored to their own evidence
sections.text: Beyond entity strings, the protocol scores a three-tier evidence hit rate (EHR): whether the segment carrying an extraction actually contains the evidence it claims, at graded evidence-similarity thresholds. EHR is low overall (macro 0.19–0.51 across models, splits, and thresholds: test-split @0.95 = 0.235 GLM-5.3-Flash / 0.371 DeepSeek-V4-Flash / 0.396 GPT-6.1-Sol), with DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s evidence sentences leading GLM-5.3-Flash’s by about + 0.14 +0.14 — the evidence-capability gap exceeds the extraction-capability gap, and even the flagship stays below 0.5. The cause is a value-vs-sentence misalignment (models emit canonical technique names where reports use natural-language descriptions; decomposition in the appendix), and the scope is verbatim-anchored, stricter than and incomparable to RAGAS-style faithfulness — explanation reliability is the current weak spot of LLM extraction , independent of entity precision. Figure 1: Coverage–accuracy curves of confidence tiering (test split): rows are GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Flash; columns are APT / CVE / AV. Orange circles: verbalized self-report; blue squares: SC frequency; gray dotted: overall accuracy. SC-frequency tiering is steep and monotone (e.g. DeepSeek-V4-Flash APT precision 0.500 at 30% coverage vs overall 0.321); verbalized is nearly flat (97%+ of self-reports pile into 80–100).

sections.heading: 4.5 Finding 4: none of it verifies truth
sections.text: Perturbation Outcome DeepSeek-V4-Flash GLM-5.3-Flash neg (retraction) true CVE abandoned 34.1% 76.2% bg (unrelated) fake CVE bound to event 26.7% 4.5% mis (attribution) injected CVE bound 95.6% 100% mis (attribution) injected org. accepted 73.3% 95.6% Control: assertion (v1), fake CVE bound 86.7% 97.8% Table 4: Relation-level counterfactuals: one injected sentence per report (all 45 targets, both models). Retained high confidence after binding: verbalized 58–98, SC frequency 0.50–0.90. If confidence measured truth, sentences that change the facts should change the scores. They do not (flash tier; the flagship counterfactual batch was not run, see Limitations). All perturbations are synthetic by construction — injected assertions contradict the facts, gold never updates, and nothing is extrapolated to real retraction or attribution-update streams. Injecting one style-matched sentence per report (Table 4 ): an attribution assertion makes both models rebind the event to an injected organization at high confidence (73.3% / 95.6%); even a sentence explicitly flagged as unrelated to this case still binds a fake vulnerability in 26.7% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) of targets, and every residual binding carries above-average confidence (verbalized 98.1 / SC 0.774). Symmetrically, one retraction sentence erases the true vulnerability from 34.1% / 76.2% of outputs while majority sampling still reproduces it — true and fake entities are symmetric in their exposure to surface text. The fake entity’s mean self-reported confidence (98.0 / 85.6) is indistinguishable from the true entity’s, and its SC frequency is identical across models (0.892): SC frequency measures textual consistency, not fact . Self-verification does not rescue this: DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s verify signal ranks at + 0.154 +0.154 on actors, its “event-related” rate on mentioned FPs (92.5%) matching true entities (93.3%) — it mistakes mention for relevance — while GLM-5.3-Flash’s verifier retains discrimination (87.1% vs. 50.1%; verify alone + 0.371 +0.371 , SC × \times verify + 0.413 +0.413 , the best actor ranker of all signals), and a third-party calibrated decision model (TypeSafe Jev; 1,461 calls, $0.051; protocol and per-call logs in the appendix) shows the same law: its increment depends on whether its window-level judgment semantics align with report-level gold. Across all tested signals — self-report, sampling consistency, self-verification, third-party verification — none survives relation-level counterfactuals : confidence sets review priorities; it must never adjudicate truth, and a verification component earns its place only when the verifier passes a one-shot FP-mentioned event-relevance precheck.

sections.heading: 4.6 Repair and generalization boundaries
sections.text: Retrieval-augmented and chain-of-thought repair helps actors (up to + 0.133 +0.133 macro-F1) and never helps vulnerabilities ( Δ ≤ ± 0.011 \Delta\leq\pm 0.011 , corroborated by an independent dual-gold recheck on a separate CVE corpus ( CIRCL, 2024 ) ); primary-entity schema alignment repairs actor over-extraction only ( + 0.111 +0.111 and + 0.167 +0.167 ) — repairs work when matched to the failure mode, consistent with Finding 2, and gains do not transfer across models (CoT flips sign on attack techniques). On an unfamiliar 2022–2025 corpus (30 group-deduplicated reports, three-tier annotation-derived gold), ranking-gain transfer is confirmed (top-30% gains positive in 6/6 cells, never below the main pool; AURC improves across the board), while fixed thresholds do not transfer: after per-corpus quantile recalibration (unlabeled percentile cut points only), threshold buckets transfer fully for attack techniques (all recalibrated gaps ≤ 0.09 \leq 0.09 ) and, for actors and vulnerabilities, cross-corpus differences are corpus-difficulty-driven with a conservative bias — threshold recalibration is a mandatory deployment step, not an option . Cross-model ranking agreement persists on the new corpus (Spearman 0.63–0.77), and a top-10 report-level audit finds the top SC bucket carries analyst value (8/10 TTP-rich, none low) with no per-report guarantee. The deployable workflow follows: triage in descending textfreq_sc order with per-type budgets — a 20% focused review zone plus tail sampling for vulnerabilities (bucket precision 0.17–0.19 vs overall 0.05–0.06), mandatory human review of the actor head (0.64–0.73 vs overall 0.27–0.32) — protocol reproducibility belongs on review checklists for extraction papers, and tiering prioritizes governance queues while evidence checks gate ingested claims. These are review-simulation figures, not measured human effort (Limitations).

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We turned the “unreliable” verdict on LLM entity extraction into a measured, preregistered account: the dominant failure is background contamination (65.6%) and gold-scope gaps (19.9%), not hallucination (1.2%); confidence signals are real but decompose into consistency, ranking, and calibration — each useful, each type-dependent, none truth-tracking under flash-tier relation-level counterfactuals. The deployable boundary is correspondingly concrete: match the ranking signal to the entity type, recalibrate thresholds per corpus, and treat confidence tiering as review prioritization with humans or independent verifiers retaining truth. All protocol, code, frozen outputs, and annotation artifacts accompany this preprint and will be made public; an anonymized copy is additionally available to reviewers.

sections.heading: Domain scope of the testbed.
sections.text: All absolute numbers come from one domain (threat-intelligence reports) and one gold-annotation convention (primary entities per campaign). We argue the mechanisms (background contamination, signal–type matching, ranks-not-verifies) generalize, and corroborate direction on a newer corpus with independent annotation-derived gold; but cross-domain replication (biomedical, legal, scientific IE) is future work, and absolute precision values are not comparable across annotation scopes.

sections.heading: Measurement scope.
sections.text: The serving gateways strip log-probabilities, so calibration proxies are signals that require no logits (verbalized + SC frequency), per the preregistered fallback plan; logprob-scope calibration awaits a direct-API environment. Gold covers three entity types — campaign attribution is unscored (free-text names without comparable ground truth). Campaign-to-report alignment covers 88.4% (18 unresolved cross-case surveys and 39 third-party group-level reports remain); no reported number depends on any single alignment, and sensitivity is recomputable from the open scripts. During one ablation round, 15 campaigns were blocked by a vendor content policy on a single channel (figures reported on the joint 84-report scope) — CTI content itself can trigger LLM content policies, a production constraint on direct deployment.

sections.heading: LLM-assisted annotation.
sections.text: The three-tier labels are produced by two LLM annotators from vendors outside the evaluated set plus a third adjudicator model — disclosed as such throughout, never as two human annotators. Agreement meets the preregistered line ( κ = 0.79 \kappa=0.79 borderline-excluded) but LLM annotation carries unknown failure modes relative to expert humans; the conservative adjudication rule resolves ambiguity toward the model-unfavorable side, and the generalization-corpus gold (lower κ \kappa , 0.53 borderline-excluded) bounds the confidence of that extrapolation. A human spot-check of a subsample is planned for the revision.

sections.heading: Model-tier coverage.
sections.text: Subjects are two new-generation low-cost (“flash”-tier) models; the flagship control covers the main table, calibration, and mention census, but not the counterfactual, verification-signal, or generalization batches (cost-prohibitive at flagship rates; scope notes mark every affected table). Conclusions about verification signals are therefore scoped to the flash tier plus one third-party verifier.

sections.heading: Calibration scope.
sections.text: We never fit a parametric calibrator; ECE/Brier/AURC are measured, not post-hoc corrected. The three-tier recalibration uses a stratified subsample whose absolute values are not comparable to full-scope tables — only the direction of scope sensitivity is claimed.

sections.heading: Corpus time boundary.
sections.text: Main-corpus collection ends around 2021; the newer-corpus experiment (§ 4.6 ) partially tests time sensitivity (entity density flat at two-year granularity, ranking consistency preserved), but extrapolating main-table precision and calibration numbers — and any fixed threshold — beyond that distribution demands caution. Keeping the corpus is deliberate: the critical audit’s numbers share its source and split, so the “unreliability not repaired” comparison stands.

sections.heading: No third-party pipeline reproduction.
sections.text: Following the reproducibility audit (5 of 12 systems re-runnable; F1 drifts of 0.16–0.70 across protocols), we re-execute no third-party pipeline as a same-scope baseline; cross-system numbers are quoted only from the critical audit under an explicitly different scope and never placed in one table with ours — our frozen one-click reproduction addresses the missing baseline at the protocol level rather than the system level.

sections.heading: Preregistered hypothesis register status.
sections.text: H1–H3 completed as reported (§ 4.2 –§ 4.4 ); H4 completed (§ 4.6 ); H5 completed with scope limits (cost anchors archived, measured human hours future work); H6 completed (§ 4.5 ). Human-efficiency measurement of the analyst triage workflow (as opposed to simulated review budgets) and an independent held-out calibration set remain unexecuted; they are registered as pending, not claimed. Remaining gold-bearing generalization candidates (a STIX 2.1 structured set, CTI-HAL, CyberNER, RAGRecon) are queued for a later stage. A channel interruption during the revision round was fully recovered and disclosed (all batches completed: counterfactuals 1,080/1,080 per model; verification 1,221+1,200 calls with 0 failures; flagship 822/822 with 0 failures); call-level logs are in the repository.

sections.heading: Data availability.
sections.text: All frozen batch outputs, evaluation code, annotation artifacts (the freeze JSON files with per-item labels and adjudication logs), and the derived gold are released through an anonymized repository for review, public upon acceptance; the report corpus is Zenodo deposit 7357568 (MIT) and the 2022–2025 corpus is the public Hugging Face dataset apt-cti-reports (MIT); redistribution of model outputs is governed by vendor terms.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.20417v1 [cs.CL] 14 Oct 2026 From Unreliable to Usable: Decomposing Failure Modes and Confidence Signals in LLM Entity Extraction — Evidence from Cyber Threat Intelligence Jiahong Qian Affiliation: Shanghai Jian Qiao University, Shanghai, China Abstract Audits of large language model (LLM) extraction from full-length documents report severe unreliability, leaving two questions open: what the failures actually consist of, and whether confidence signals can turn unreliable output into usable output. We run a preregistered, fully frozen evaluation of two new-generation low-cost LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash) with a flagship-tier control (GPT-6.1-Sol) on a public corpus of 354 incident campaigns (315 unique reports, 630 model–report evaluations), scoring extraction quality against gold, confidence calibration, and robustness to single-sentence perturbations. Three findings emerge. (1) Unreliability persists across tiers: micro precision is 0.03–0.34 and verbalized calibration error (ECE) 0.53–0.94 across both splits; the gap does not close at the flagship tier. (2) The dominant failure is not hallucination: a full mention census plus a three-tier annotation of 360 sampled candidates (two independent LLM annotators from vendors outside the evaluated set, Cohen’s κ = 0.79 \kappa=0.79 on the preregistered acceptance line, fully disclosed) back-projects to 65.6% background mentions and 19.9% gold-scope gaps, with only 1.2% unsupported candidates. (3) Confidence ranks but does not verify: zero-cost self-consistency-frequency tiering passes a preregistered top-30% precision-gain bar in all six test-split model–type cells (4/6 on train), the zero-cost text-frequency × \times SC combination wins 3, ties 2, loses 1 across cells, yet relation-level counterfactuals on all 45 targets show that a single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in 95.6–100% of cases, and even a background sentence explicitly marked as unrelated still binds a fake vulnerability in up to 26.7% of them. We conclude with a deployment boundary: confidence tiering may set review priorities, never truth. 1 Introduction When large language models (LLMs) fail at information extraction, the failures are commonly attributed to hallucination. Auditing 315 unique real-world documents (354 incident campaigns; 630 model–report evaluation runs) under a frozen, preregistered protocol with three-tier verified annotation, we find hallucination accounts for only 1.2% of false positives — 65.6% are background mentions : correct strings extracted from the wrong context. We then ask whether confidence signals can still make such a system usable, and show they rank but do not verify : across all 45 counterfactual targets, a single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in 95.6–100% of cases, and one background sentence explicitly marked as unrelated still binds a fake vulnerability in up to 26.7%. These results address a question that outlives any single domain, and the stakes are concrete. LLM-based extraction pipelines for structured threat intelligence claimed 83–97% precision ( Chen et al., 2024 ) ; a critical audit ( Mezzi et al., 2025a ) traced those numbers to toy inputs of 18–106 words and showed that at real scale recall falls below 0.80 and calibration worsens; a reproducibility audit found only 5 of 12 extraction systems re-runnable under their published protocols ( Hakim and Song, 2026 ) . But “unreliable” is a verdict, not a diagnosis — and verbalized confidence is itself severely miscalibrated ( Xiong et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2017 ) . It does not say which part of the pipeline is broken — the model’s faithfulness, the evaluation scope, or the task definition — and it does not say whether the residual uncertainty can be managed. Two questions follow. First, what is the failure made of? Hallucinated content, wrong context, or a mismatch between what the model extracts and what the annotation counts as correct demand different repairs. Second, can confidence make unreliability usable? If high-confidence outputs can be prioritized for scarce human review, an unreliable extractor may still be deployable — unless confidence itself is untrustworthy. We answer both questions on a testbed chosen for measurement quality rather than topical breadth: cyber threat intelligence (CTI) reports, long documents describing intrusion campaigns, from which models must extract three entity types (threat-actor groups, vulnerability identifiers, attack techniques). The domain offers three assets that generic extraction benchmarks rarely combine: a public corpus with gold annotations for 354 campaigns ( Di Tizio et al., 2022 ) , a published critical audit whose protocol and splits we reuse so results are directly comparable ( Mezzi et al., 2025a ) , and a real deployment need — security analysts already triage extracted indicators by confidence, so “usable” has an operational meaning. Our evaluation protocol is explicit and frozen end to end: multiset entity matching with alias equivalence classes, dual confidence proxies (verbalized self-report and self-consistency frequency under 5-sample resampling), preregistered acceptance thresholds, relation-level counterfactual perturbations, and a three-tier annotation study (textual mention / event relevance / relation correctness) on 360 stratified candidates, labeled by two independent LLM annotators from vendors outside the evaluated set with adjudication fully disclosed ( κ = 0.79 \kappa=0.79 on the borderline-excluded preregistered line). Findings. (1) Unreliability persists across model tiers. Micro precision spans 0.03–0.34 against recall of 0.81–0.99; verbalized ECE is 0.53–0.94 across both splits, and a full-scope control at the flagship tier (GPT-6.1-Sol) shows the same pattern (0.63–0.94). (2) The dominant failure is background contamination, not hallucination. 99.7–99.8% of false positives have an explicit textual source in the report; weighted back-projection of the three-tier annotation yields 65.6% background mentions and 19.9% gold-scope gaps against 1.2% unsupported candidates. (3) Confidence signals decompose into separable, entity-type-dependent properties. SC frequency passes a preregistered ranking bar in all six test-split model–type cells (4/6 on train, with both vulnerability cells just under the line); controlling for text frequency, its partial correlation with correctness is significant in 6/6 groups ( r = 0.30 r=0.30 – 0.43 0.43 ); mention strength tracks event centrality for actors while sampling stability tracks correctness for vulnerabilities and techniques. (4) No confidence signal measures truth. A single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in 95.6–100% of 45 counterfactual targets; verification signals — self-run or third-party — inherit the same blindness; repairs only help when matched to the failure mode, ranking gains transfer to a newer corpus, and thresholds must be recalibrated per corpus. Contributions. This is a systematic evaluation study: model choices and prompting configurations are experimental settings, ranking heuristics are baselines, error analysis and counterfactuals are the core explanation, and repair experiments serve the boundary characterization. The contributions are three: • A reproducible reliability measurement. To our knowledge (as of 2026-10, within audited coverage), the first evaluation framework merging multiset PRF with alias equivalence classes, dual-proxy calibration, three-tier evidence annotation, and preregistered thresholds into one explicit, frozen protocol — executed on the public audit corpus as a direct response to the reproducibility audit above. All protocol, code, and frozen evaluation outputs accompany this preprint and will be made public; an anonymized copy is additionally available to reviewers as supplementary material. • A quantified failure-mode decomposition. A full-scope mention census plus a preregistered three-tier annotation study locating 85.5% of the false-positive mass in background mentions and gold-scope gaps, against 1.2% hallucination — reframing “LLMs hallucinate entities” as “LLMs over-attend to context”. • A tested deployment boundary. Evidence across confidence signals from self-report to third-party verifiers that ranking benefit is real, signal–type matching matters, calibration scope matters, and no tested signal survives relation-level counterfactuals; ranking gain transfers to a newer corpus while thresholds must be recalibrated. 2 Related Work Calibration and verbalized uncertainty. Classical calibration is measured by ECE and reliability curves ( Guo et al., 2017 ) ; for LLMs, verbalized confidence is often miscalibrated ( Xiong et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2023 ) , sampling consistency carries partial signal ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Kadavath et al., 2022 ) , and selective prediction formalizes the risk–coverage trade-off our tiering analysis instantiates ( Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017 ) . We add a three-way distinction — output consistency , ranking benefit , and probabilistic calibration are different quantities that must not be conflated — and test all three against counterfactual ground truth. LLM-based extraction from threat intelligence. Structured extraction from CTI reports attracted rapid LLM adoption ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Mouiche and Saad, 2026 ; Bouchiha and Blanc, 2026 ) alongside benchmarks ( Alam et al., 2024 ; Ji et al., 2024 ; Alam et al., 2025 ; Ryan et al., 2026 ; Valletta et al., 2026 ) and corpora ( Di Tizio et al., 2022 ; Ech-Chammakhy et al., 2025 ; Das et al., 2026 ) . A critical audit ( Mezzi et al., 2025a ) overturned headline extraction numbers by exposing scoring loopholes and finding LLMs unreliable with overconfidence; follow-ups target pipeline dependencies ( Berriche et al., 2026 ) , automated TTP and strategic-intelligence extraction ( Cheng et al., 2026 ; Ech-Chammakhy et al., 2026 ) , agentic KG construction ( Li et al., 2026 ) , calibrated verification services ( Vasan et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) , and corpus fragmentation ( Suarez-Roman et al., 2026 ) . Reproducibility audits question KG-construction pipelines ( Dinis et al., 2025 ; Hakim and Song, 2026 ) , and systems such as CTINexus ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) have been re-examined under stricter scoring; Chen et al. (2024) systematizes the application landscape. Our work is a systematic evaluation study on the audit’s own public corpus: we reuse its splits for comparability, and extend the audit line from “unreliable” to a measured, preregistered account of what the unreliability consists of and where confidence helps. Failure-mode analysis of extraction. Prior CTI work reports misses, over-extraction, and misbinding qualitatively ( Alam et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Mezzi et al., 2025b ; Heo et al., 2026 ) . We quantitatively decompose false positives into mention-level and event-level layers with a preregistered three-tier annotation, and separate hallucination (1.2%) from background contamination (65.6%) and gold-scope gaps (19.9%). 3 Experimental Setup 3.1 Task, corpus, and models Given a full-length CTI report, the model extracts three entity types: threat-actor groups (APT), vulnerability identifiers (CVE), and attack techniques (AV, MITRE ATT&CK-style names ( Strom et al., 2020 ) ). We use the public Di Tizio corpus ( Di Tizio et al., 2022 ) under the exact campaign-level 70/30 split of the critical audit ( Mezzi et al., 2025a ) : 354 campaigns (248 train / 106 test at campaign level), 315 train and 93 test reports per model — the same report split reused for both models, for 630 model–report runs in total; Table 1 reports the test split. Gold follows the corpus’s STIX 2.1 structure ( OASIS, 2021 ) and marks primary entities per campaign. We evaluate two new-generation low-cost models (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash — the cheapest “flash” service tiers of their vendors) as subjects and GPT-6.1-Sol as a flagship-tier full-scope control; all runs use frozen prompts, segmentation (cap 40k tokens, overlap 800), temperature-0 extraction with 5-sample self-consistency (SC) resampling (T = = 0.7) per segment. Every reported number is regenerated from frozen batch outputs; the pipeline records gateway and model identity per call (6,048 used segment-level calls on the main table; full call/token accounting in the appendix). 3.2 Scoring and confidence signals Multiset matching with alias equivalence classes. Predictions and gold are matched as multisets under type-specific normalization: alias equivalence classes with word/digit boundaries (APT), fault-tolerant CVE regexes covering PDF mojibake separators and legacy CAN- prefixes, and a conservative 13-value AV synonym table. This counts every mention as a prediction while gold lists primary entities — a deliberately strict-on-the-model scope whose FP semantics is disambiguated by the annotation study (§ 4.2 ). Confidence signals. (1) Verbalized : the model’s self-reported 0–100 confidence; (2) SC frequency ( sc_freq ): the share of 5 resamples reproducing the entity — a zero-extra-cost measure of output consistency; (3) text frequency : the count of the entity string in the report, a black-box signal requiring no logits. Their rank-percentile mean forms the zero-cost combination textfreq_sc ; two external verifiers (self-verification and a third-party calibrated decision model) are evaluated against these in § 4.4 . Preregistered acceptance. Before evaluation we registered: a tiering bar (top-30% confidence-bucket precision ≥ \geq overall + 0.10 +0.10 ), an annotation agreement line ( κ ≥ 0.7 \kappa\geq 0.7 ), and a hypothesis register (H1–H6) separating measured claims from pending ones. Failing a registered bar must be restated as a negative result. 3.3 Three-tier annotation of sampled candidates To separate what the model extracted from what the annotation counts , all evaluation units of the test split were partitioned by a deliberately lenient mention detector into TP / FP-mentioned / FP-unsupported, and a 360-row stratified subsample (60 per model × \times type; the FP-unsupported stratum fully sampled, the rest balanced across SC-frequency tertiles) was labeled on three tiers: L1 textual mention (does the string appear), L2 event relevance (does it belong to this incident, not background or related work), L3 relation correctness (is the binding and attribution right). The second-annotator role was filled by two independent LLMs (kimi-k3, minimax-m3; neither vendor is among the evaluated models ) under a frozen prompt with temperature 0 and golden-item gating; 36 hard disagreements went to a third adjudicator model and 27 borderline items to a conservative rule resolving toward the model-unfavorable side. On an unfamiliar 2022–2025 corpus (30 group-deduplicated reports, three-tier annotation-derived gold), ranking-gain transfer is confirmed (top-30% gains positive in 6/6 cells, never below the main pool; AURC improves across the board), while fixed thresholds do not transfer: after per-corpus quantile recalibration (unlabeled percentile cut points only), threshold buckets transfer fully for attack techniques (all recalibrated gaps ≤ 0.09 \leq 0.09 ) and, for actors and vulnerabilities, cross-corpus differences are corpus-difficulty-driven with a conservative bias — threshold recalibration is a mandatory deployment step, not an option . Cross-model ranking agreement persists on the new corpus (Spearman 0.63–0.77), and a top-10 report-level audit finds the top SC bucket carries analyst value (8/10 TTP-rich, none low) with no per-report guarantee. The deployable workflow follows: triage in descending textfreq_sc order with per-type budgets — a 20% focused review zone plus tail sampling for vulnerabilities (bucket precision 0.17–0.19 vs overall 0.05–0.06), mandatory human review of the actor head (0.64–0.73 vs overall 0.27–0.32) — protocol reproducibility belongs on review checklists for extraction papers, and tiering prioritizes governance queues while evidence checks gate ingested claims. These are review-simulation figures, not measured human effort (Limitations). 5 Conclusion We turned the “unreliable” verdict on LLM entity extraction into a measured, preregistered account: the dominant failure is background contamination (65.6%) and gold-scope gaps (19.9%), not hallucination (1.2%); confidence signals are real but decompose into consistency, ranking, and calibration — each useful, each type-dependent, none truth-tracking under flash-tier relation-level counterfactuals. The deployable boundary is correspondingly concrete: match the ranking signal to the entity type, recalibrate thresholds per corpus, and treat confidence tiering as review prioritization with humans or independent verifiers retaining truth. All protocol, code, frozen outputs, and annotation artifacts accompany this preprint and will be made public; an anonymized copy is additionally available to reviewers. 6 Limitations Domain scope of the testbed. All absolute numbers come from one domain (threat-intelligence reports) and one gold-annotation convention (primary entities per campaign). We argue the mechanisms (background contamination, signal–type matching, ranks-not-verifies) generalize, and corroborate direction on a newer corpus with independent annotation-derived gold; but cross-domain replication (biomedical, legal, scientific IE) is future work, and absolute precision values are not comparable across annotation scopes. Measurement scope. The serving gateways strip log-probabilities, so calibration proxies are signals that require no logits (verbalized + SC frequency), per the preregistered fallback plan; logprob-scope calibration awaits a direct-API environment. Gold covers three entity types — campaign attribution is unscored (free-text names without comparable ground truth). Campaign-to-report alignment covers 88.4% (18 unresolved cross-case surveys and 39 third-party group-level reports remain); no reported number depends on any single alignment, and sensitivity is recomputable from the open scripts. During one ablation round, 15 campaigns were blocked by a vendor content policy on a single channel (figures reported on the joint 84-report scope) — CTI content itself can trigger LLM content policies, a production constraint on direct deployment. LLM-assisted annotation. The three-tier labels are produced by two LLM annotators from vendors outside the evaluated set plus a third adjudicator model — disclosed as such throughout, never as two human annotators. Agreement meets the preregistered line ( κ = 0.79 \kappa=0.79 borderline-excluded) but LLM annotation carries unknown failure modes relative to expert humans; the conservative adjudication rule resolves ambiguity toward the model-unfavorable side, and the generalization-corpus gold (lower κ \kappa , 0.53 borderline-excluded) bounds the confidence of that extrapolation. A human spot-check of a subsample is planned for the revision. Model-tier coverage. Subjects are two new-generation low-cost (“flash”-tier) models; the flagship control covers the main table, calibration, and mention census, but not the counterfactual, verification-signal, or generalization batches (cost-prohibitive at flagship rates; scope notes mark every affected table). Conclusions about verification signals are therefore scoped to the flash tier plus one third-party verifier. Calibration scope. We never fit a parametric calibrator; ECE/Brier/AURC are measured, not post-hoc corrected. The three-tier recalibration uses a stratified subsample whose absolute values are not comparable to full-scope tables — only the direction of scope sensitivity is claimed. Corpus time boundary. Main-corpus collection ends around 2021; the newer-corpus experiment (§ 4.6 ) partially tests time sensitivity (entity density flat at two-year granularity, ranking consistency preserved), but extrapolating main-table precision and calibration numbers — and any fixed threshold — beyond that distribution demands caution. Keeping the corpus is deliberate: the critical audit’s numbers share its source and split, so the “unreliability not repaired” comparison stands. No third-party pipeline reproduction. Following the reproducibility audit (5 of 12 systems re-runnable; F1 drifts of 0.16–0.70 across protocols), we re-execute no third-party pipeline as a same-scope baseline; cross-system numbers are quoted only from the critical audit under an explicitly different scope and never placed in one table with ours — our frozen one-click reproduction addresses the missing baseline at the protocol level rather than the system level. Preregistered hypothesis register status. H1–H3 completed as reported (§ 4.2 –§ 4.4 ); H4 completed (§ 4.6 ); H5 completed with scope limits (cost anchors archived, measured human hours future work); H6 completed (§ 4.5 ). Human-efficiency measurement of the analyst triage workflow (as opposed to simulated review budgets) and an independent held-out calibration set remain unexecuted; they are registered as pending, not claimed. Remaining gold-bearing generalization candidates (a STIX 2.1 structured set, CTI-HAL, CyberNER, RAGRecon) are queued for a later stage.
